title: Episode 220: Russia: Peter the Great, the Window to the West, and the Founding of St. Petersburg

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. Today, our journey through the great nations of Europe takes us to the vast, snow-swept plains of Russia, and to the colossal six-foot-eight tsar who seized a medieval, isolated realm by the collar and dragged it kicking and screaming into the modern world: Peter the Great.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE GIANT TSAR AND THE GERMAN QUARTER OF MOSCOW
In the late seventeenth century, Russia was an isolated, deeply conservative Orthodox kingdom, cut off from the scientific, maritime, and intellectual currents transforming Western Europe. The Kremlin of Moscow was dominated by long-bearded boyars in heavy brocade robes and the fierce, reactionary palace musketeers known as the Streltsy. Into this cloistered world was born Peter Romanov, a physical giant who grew to six feet eight inches tall, possessed of demonic physical energy, boundless curiosity, and a complete disdain for traditional court etiquette. Rather than studying liturgical texts, young Peter spent his youth roaming the German Quarter of Moscow—a vibrant enclave of foreign merchants, artisans, and mercenary soldiers. There, he absorbed foreign languages, studied geometry, and fell passionately in love with Western firearms and sailing vessels. In the nearby fields of Preobrazhenskoye, Peter assembled two mock regiments of neighborhood youths, drilling them in modern European tactics, unaware that these boyhood playmates would become the elite imperial guards who would reshape Russian history. From his early encounters in the German Quarter, Peter grasped a fundamental truth: Russia could never survive as a great power while chained to the superstitious traditions of its past.  In his youth, Peter discovered an abandoned English sailboat rotting in a barn at Izmaylovo, an encounter that sparked his lifelong obsession with sailing and navigation, prompting him to learn how to tack against the wind from a Dutch master.  In Moscow's German Quarter, Peter befriended Patrick Gordon, a shrewd Scottish general, and Franz Lefort, a charismatic Swiss adventurer, who introduced the impressionable prince to Western military tactics, shipbuilding, and modern European thought.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE GRAND EMBASSY INCOGNITO TO THE WEST: 1697–1698
In 1697, Peter did something no Russian monarch had ever dared to do: he left his country to travel across Western Europe on an unprecedented diplomatic and scientific mission known as the Grand Embassy. To avoid stifling diplomatic ceremonies, the giant monarch traveled under the humble pseudonym of 'Peter Mikhailov', an ordinary non-commissioned officer in the diplomatic retinue. In the Netherlands, Peter settled in the Dutch port town of Zaandam, renting a modest wooden hut, putting on a carpenter's rough apron, and working with an adze and mallet at the East India Company shipyards to master the science of naval architecture. In London, Peter studied royal artillery at Woolwich, observed parliamentary debates in Westminster, and lived at Deptford docks, wrecking the house of diarist John Evelyn during boisterous late-night drinking bouts with his companions. He recruited hundreds of Western shipwrights, engineers, navigators, surgeons, and artillery officers, stuffing crates full of navigational sextants, surgical instruments, and clockwork mechanisms to haul back to Moscow. The Grand Embassy was an intellectual shock to the young tsar, convincing him that modern technological mastery, naval command, and administrative discipline were the only instruments that could preserve Russian sovereignty.  While in England, King William III was so impressed by Peter's technical curiosity that he gifted him the royal yacht Royal Transport, equipped with twenty modern bronze brass cannons, which Peter personally sailed through Channel gales.  Peter's time at Deptford dockyard on the Thames allowed him to observe the Royal Navy's state-of-the-art timber preservation and sailmaking techniques, which he later incorporated into the Admiralty shipyards of St. Petersburg.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE REBELLION OF THE STRELTSY AND THE SEVERED BEARDS
Peter's grand European tour was cut short in 1698 by terrifying news: the conservative Streltsy regiments had revolted, marching on Moscow to overthrow the modernizing tsar and restore traditional Muscovite ways. Rushing home across Poland, Peter arrived in Moscow with cold fury. The rebellion was brutally crushed outside the capital, but Peter was determined to eradicate the old order forever. The morning after his return, the boyars gathered at the Kremlin to welcome their sovereign, falling to their knees in customary reverence. Without uttering a word, Peter produced a heavy pair of barber's shears and personally began hacking off the cherished, flowing beards of his highest aristocrats—an act of religious sacrilege in traditional Orthodox eyes. He decreed that all Russian nobility, merchants, and civil servants must shave their faces or pay a punishing annual 'beard tax', receiving a bronze token stamped with the words 'Tax Paid' and 'The Beard is a Superfluous Burden'. Traditional floor-length robes were banned in favor of practical Hungarian and French coats. When the Streltsy rebels were brought to the execution grounds, Peter demanded that his own courtiers wield the executioner's axes, breaking the political back of medieval Muscovy in a single stroke of despotic violence.  The beard tax was strictly enforced by imperial inspectors stationed at every town gate, who mercilessly sheared the beards of stubborn peasants and merchants who could not produce their bronze or silver exemption coins.  Boyars who stubbornly refused to shave their beards were subjected to public ridicule, forced to wear special donkey-fur collars and paraded through the streets of Moscow as backward relics of a discarded past.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE GREAT NORTHERN WAR AND THE DISASTER OF NARVA
To open a maritime trading window to Europe, Peter needed an ice-free port on the Baltic Sea, which had been turned into a virtual 'Swedish lake' by the formidable military empire of Sweden. In 1700, Peter forged an alliance with Denmark and Poland-Saxony, launching the Great Northern War against the newly crowned eighteen-year-old King Charles XII of Sweden. The campaign began in total catastrophe: at the Battle of Narva in November 1700, Charles XII led a vastly outnumbered Swedish army through a blinding snowstorm, shattering the ill-trained Russian army in minutes and capturing all their artillery. European courts mocked the Russian tsar as a savage barbarian who could never match modern European discipline. But Peter was never more dangerous than in defeat. 'The Swedes will beat us again and again,' he calmly observed, 'but in the end, they will teach us how to beat them.' He melted down church bells across Russia to cast hundreds of new bronze cannons, conscripted thousands of peasants into lifelong military service, and subjected his recruits to rigorous, modern European drill under foreign officers, forging a new imperial army in the fires of national crisis.  At Narva, Charles XII captured hundreds of Russian officers, who were paraded through Stockholm as trophies, but Peter refused to despair, converting monastic silver and bronze parish bells into over three hundred brand-new field guns within a single year.  Peter's decree conscripting one peasant recruit from every twenty households created a permanent standing army of two hundred thousand disciplined soldiers, bound to lifelong service under the direct command of the crown.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE MIRACULOUS VICTORY AT POLTAVA: 1709
Nine years after Narva, King Charles XII invaded the Russian heartland with his legendary, undefeated Swedish army, marching toward Moscow through the bitter Russian winter. Peter adopted a ruthless scorched-earth strategy, burning crops, poisoning wells, and denying the invaders food and shelter. By the summer of 1709, the exhausted, frostbitten Swedish forces were pinned down besieging the fortress town of Poltava in Ukraine. On June 27, 1709, the two armies met in one of the decisive clashes of world history. Peter rode through the Russian ranks in his simple Preobrazhensky uniform, a bullet piercing his tricorn hat, inspiring his soldiers with the shout that they were fighting not for Peter, but for the existence of Russia herself. The reformed Russian infantry, supported by synchronized artillery barrages, stood their ground against the ferocious Swedish charges, outflanking and encircling Charles XII's elite regiments. The Swedish army was annihilated; King Charles fled into exile in the Ottoman Empire. The victory at Poltava shocked the courts of Europe: in a single summer morning, Sweden was displaced as the dominant military power of Northern Europe, and Russia emerged onto the world stage as an unstoppable imperial colossus.  At Poltava, the sweltering Ukrainian heat and lack of ammunition crippled the Swedish charges, allowing Peter's synchronized artillery batteries to fire grapeshot into the Swedish flanks with devastating, surgical efficiency.  The Swedish field marshal Carl Gustav Rehnskiöld was captured at Poltava alongside thousands of Swedish officers, whom Peter magnanimously invited to dine with him in his imperial tent, toasting them as his 'teachers in the art of war'.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE WINDOW TO THE WEST: BUILDING ST. PETERSBURG UPON THE SWAMPS
Even as the war with Sweden raged, Peter undertook the most audacious civil engineering project in European history: the construction of a brand-new imperial capital from the desolate marshes where the Neva River emptied into the Gulf of Finland. Begun in May 1703 with the founding of the Peter and Paul Fortress, the city of St. Petersburg was conceived as Peter's 'Window to the West'—a modern, grid-planned European city of stone palaces, wide canals, and naval wharves that turned its back on the ancient traditions of Moscow. The cost in human suffering was staggering: tens of thousands of conscripted serfs, Swedish prisoners of war, and Cossack laborers dug the freezing mud with bare hands, dragging heavy granite boulders across bogs without wheelbarrows. Epidemics of malaria, dysentery, and typhus swept the camps, killing an estimated forty thousand laborers whose bones were buried beneath the city's foundations, earning it the grim epithet 'the city built on bones'. Peter compelled every cart entering the city to bring a quota of stones, and forbade any stone building anywhere else in Russia so all masons would be forced to work on St. Petersburg. By 1712, Peter declared St. Petersburg the official capital of Russia, moving the entire royal court and foreign embassies to the glittering new city by the sea.  St. Petersburg's grand avenues were modeled on the canals of Amsterdam and the baroque vistas of Versailles, requiring every nobleman owning over thirty serfs to build a stone townhouse along the icy banks of the Moika and Fontanka canals.  The construction of St. Petersburg proceeded under Peter's direct supervision: the tsar lived in a tiny, three-room wooden cabin painted to resemble Dutch brick, overseeing the pile-driving of thousands of oak foundations into the muddy swamp.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE EMPEROR OF ALL RUSSIA AND THE LEGACY OF MODERNIZATION
In 1721, after twenty-one years of relentless warfare, the Treaty of Nystad ended the Great Northern War, granting Russia permanent possession of the Baltic coastlines of Livonia, Estonia, and Ingria. The Russian Senate bestowed upon Peter the titles of 'Father of the Fatherland' and 'Peter the Great, Emperor of All Russia', officially transforming the Tsardom of Muscovy into the Russian Empire. In his final years, Peter instituted the Table of Ranks, an revolutionary meritocratic system that abolished aristocratic birthright in favor of state service, allowing commoners to attain noble rank through military valor and administrative competence. He founded the Russian Academy of Sciences, created Russia's first newspaper, established the Baltic Fleet, and rationalized provincial administration. When Peter died in January 1725 at the age of fifty-two—contracting fatal pneumonia after wading chest-deep into the icy Gulf of Finland to rescue drowning sailors from a stranded vessel—he left behind an unrecognizable realm. Through sheer iron will, terrifying brutality, and visionary genius, Peter the Great had forged a continental superpower that would dominate European geopolitics for centuries to come.  Peter's Table of Ranks fundamentally dismantled the hereditary power of the ancient boyar families, establishing fourteen civil and military ranks where promotion was earned solely through demonstrable merit, literacy, and state service.  Peter's administrative reforms established specialized governmental colleges modeled on Swedish ministries, replacing corrupt boyar assemblies with efficient bureaucratic departments overseeing commerce, justice, and foreign affairs.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. Next week, our exploration of Russian history continues with Episode 223: Catherine the Great, the Winter Palace, the Enlightenment, and the Golden Age of the Russian Empire. Until then, stay curious.
